content: Nocturia, derived from the Latin word nox (night) and the Greek word οὖρα (urine), refers to the need to wake up during the night to urinate, thereby interrupting sleep. It is also known as nycturia (from the Greek νυκτουρία). This condition is more commonly observed in elderly individuals. Nocturia may result from excessive fluid intake before bedtime or may indicate an underlying medical condition, such as chronic renal failure, urinary incontinence, interstitial cystitis, diabetes, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), ureteropelvic junction obstruction, or prostate cancer. The International Continence Society (ICS) defined nocturia in 2002 as the need to wake up one or more times during the night to void. Clinically, nocturia is defined as waking up two or more times per night to urinate. The pathophysiology of nocturia is multifactorial and may involve urological disorders, abnormalities in bladder capacity, prostate enlargement, or excessive urine production due to fluid redistribution during sleep. Other contributing factors include overproduction of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) caused by sleep apnea or congestive heart failure, dysfunction or deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or arginine vasopressin (AVP), use of diuretics, and behavioral factors such as high fluid intake at night. AVP plays a critical role in regulating urine production by promoting water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts, thereby reducing urine volume. A deficiency or dysfunction of AVP can lead to decreased urine concentration, increased urine volume, and nocturia. The causes of nocturia can be categorized based on pathogenesis, hormonal imbalances, or organ system dysfunctions. Common causes include anxiety disorders, BPH, bladder outlet obstruction, chronic renal failure, diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, interstitial cystitis, obstructive sleep apnea, and medications such as diuretics. In men, risk factors include prostatitis, BPH, and prostate cancer. In women, risk factors include high BMI, heart disease, inflammatory bowel disease, uterine prolapse, hysterectomy, menopause, and recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). The prevalence of nocturia increases with age. Among individuals aged 40 years and older, approximately 69,000 per 100,000 men and 76,000 per 100,000 women experience at least one nocturnal void. The prevalence of two or more voids per night is higher in older populations, with rates ranging from 28,000 to 62,000 per 100,000 women and 29,000 to 59,000 per 100,000 men aged 70–80 years. Nocturia affects men and women equally, although younger women are more likely to experience it than younger men, while older men are more likely to develop it than older women. Risk factors for nocturia include aging, Hispanic and Black race, a history of nocturia during childhood, pre-existing conditions such as diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, hypertension, arthritis, asthma, depression, and anxiety disorders, as well as the use of diuretics. Lifestyle factors, such as excessive fluid intake in the evening, also contribute. The diagnosis of nocturia is based on clinical history, as defined by the ICS. Patients should be asked to maintain a bladder diary, recording fluid intake, timing and volume of urination, and the number of nocturnal voids. Frequency-volume charts can also aid in diagnosis. Physical examination should include blood pressure measurement, digital rectal examination of the prostate in men, pelvic examination in women, assessment of lower limb edema, evaluation of genital abnormalities, abdominal examination for urinary retention, and calculation of BMI or waist circumference. Laboratory tests helpful in diagnosing nocturia include urinalysis with urine culture to rule out UTIs, serum electrolytes, renal function tests (BUN, creatinine, GFR), serum glucose levels, HbA1c to rule out diabetes mellitus, lipid profile, and PSA levels to rule out prostate cancer or BPH. Imaging studies, such as ultrasound, may be used to assess post-void residual volume and bladder wall thickness. Cystoscopy may be helpful in identifying bladder abnormalities. Treatment of nocturia depends on the underlying cause. Behavioral modifications include limiting fluid intake in the evening, avoiding alcohol, caffeine, and diuretics, treating underlying conditions such as diabetes or chronic constipation, elevating the lower limbs in the evening, and engaging in physical exercise. Pharmacologic therapies include desmopressin, which reduces urine volume by increasing water reabsorption in the renal tubules through vasopressin V2 receptors. Desmopressin is the preferred treatment for nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria, as recommended by the European Association of Urology (EAU). Other medications include alpha-blockers, antimuscarinics, phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, and botulinum toxin. Surgical intervention is not typically recommended for the management of nocturia and is usually reserved for patients with specific underlying conditions. Primary prevention measures include lifestyle modifications, such as reducing evening fluid and salt intake, taking afternoon naps, weight loss in obese individuals, urinating before bedtime, and using compression stockings or elevating the legs to reduce edema. There are no established measures for secondary prevention of nocturia.
